stories.title: U.S. Apartment Rents Post Eighth Consecutive Month of Growth
stories.excerpt: U.S. apartment rents were essentially flat in July, with the national average rising +0.03% to $1,747 from June’s upwardly revised level of $1,746, CoStar Group’s Apartments.com reported Wednesday. This marks the eighth consecutive month of positive rent increases following a period of flat to declining monthly performance in the second half of 2025. On an annual basis, rent growth accelerated to +1.0% in July 2026 from the upwardly revised +0.9% in June and was slightly down from the +1.1% reading recorded one year earlier. June 2026 was initially reported as a +0.1% month-over-month increase and has been revised upward to +0.2%. Although apartment rent growth typically slows as the market moves further into the summer leasing season, gains in July were particularly subdued. “Following modest rent increases during the spring, the +0.03% increase recorded in July represents a notable slowdown in monthly pricing momentum,” according to Apartments.com. “While annual rent growth continues to improve gradually, elevated supply levels continue to restrain pricing momentum nationally.” Where the apartment industry connects. Meet the owners, investors, developers, lenders, brokers, and service providers driving today’s multifamily market at Connect Apartments. Build relationships, uncover opportunities, and stay ahead of what’s next. The post U.S. Apartment Rents Post Eighth Consecutive Month of Growth appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: U.S. apartment rents +0.03% MoM in July 2026, +1.0% YoY; eighth consecutive month of positive growth.
Elevated national supply levels continue to restrain pricing momentum despite modest spring gains.
Monthly rent growth notably slowed in July despite typical summer leasing season patterns.
stories.summary: U.S. apartment rents rose +0.03% month-over-month in July 2026 to a national average of $1,747, marking the eighth straight month of positive growth. Annual rent growth accelerated to +1.0% from +0.9% in June, but monthly momentum has notably slowed. Apartments.com attributes the subdued pricing to elevated supply levels restraining the market nationally, even as spring gains had been modest.
stories.impact: Elevated supply nationally is capping rent growth at historically weak levels (+1.0% YoY), signaling that new deliveries are outpacing demand absorption. Developers should expect continued downward pricing pressure until supply-demand rebalances; new projects must compete on location and amenity differentiation rather than rent premiums. This environment favors selective development in supply-constrained submarkets with strong job growth.

stories.title: Costa Mesa Multifamily Changes Hands for Value-Add Repositioning
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of 1990 Maple Ave., a 41-unit multifamily property in Costa Mesa. The property sold for $16.9 million or $412,195 per unit, approximately $550,000 above the property’s 2018 selling price. “Sundance West Apartment Homes presented a rare opportunity to acquire a low-density multifamily community in one of Orange County’s most supply-constrained rental markets,” said Matthew Kipp, senior managing director investments. “The property’s unique concentration of two- and three-bedroom floor plans and the meaningful capital improvements completed by prior ownership, including electrical upgrades and roof replacements, attracted significant investor interest. The competitive bidding environment allowed the seller to look beyond price alone and select a buyer whose local experience provided the highest confidence in execution.” Kipp and Tyler Leeson, executive managing director investments, in Marcus & Millichap’s Orange County office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a local family, exchanging out-of-state to reduce hands-on management, and procured the buyer, a professional investor acquiring for value-add repositioning. The post Costa Mesa Multifamily Changes Hands for Value-Add Repositioning appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 41-unit Costa Mesa multifamily sold for $16.9M ($412K/unit), +$550K above 2018 price.
Property marketed as rare low-density acquisition in Orange County's supply-constrained rental market.
Buyer acquired for value-add repositioning; prior ownership completed electrical upgrades and roof replacement.
stories.summary: A 41-unit multifamily property at 1990 Maple Ave. in Costa Mesa sold for $16.9 million ($412,195/unit), approximately $550,000 above its 2018 sale price, brokered by Marcus & Millichap. The property attracted significant investor interest as a rare low-density opportunity in one of Orange County's supply-constrained markets, with two- and three-bedroom floor plans and recent capital improvements. The buyer plans value-add repositioning.
stories.impact: Costa Mesa's identified supply constraint and competitive bidding environment demonstrate strong investor appetite for scarce, well-maintained multifamily assets in Orange County. This signals durable demand in the submarket and validates rental strength; developers with land or acquisition opportunities in supply-constrained Orange County coastal/central submarkets can underwrite with confidence in sustained pricing power and buyer demand.

stories.title: NYC Issues Partial Stop-Work Order at SL Green’s 750 Third Avenue Conversion
stories.excerpt: New York City’s Department of Buildings (DOB) has halted construction work at the third office-to-conversion project in Manhattan this month. The DOB issued a partial stop-work order at SL Green Realty’s $805 million conversion project at 750 Third Avenue in Midtown East, which is set to result in 680 residential units and potentially see 11 floors added. The halt comes after the near-collapse of the former Pfizer headquarters earlier in July, when steel beams at MetroLoft and David Werner’s 235 East 42nd Street project buckled and sparked the evacuation of 10 surrounding Midtown blocks. Earlier this week, GFP Real Estate’s conversion project at 222 Broadway in the Financial District was also halted after cracks were found on a newly added floor. In the case of 750 Third Avenue, it seems as if steel columns were not welded properly and inconsistencies were reported, according to the DOB. As a result, inspectors have temporarily stopped all steel work above the eighth floor at the 34-story property, according to The New York Times, which first reported the news. “During our structural reinforcement prep work, prior to beginning any overbuild work, we identified an on-site condition that differed from the plans that were submitted to the city, which was visible only after completing initial preparation work,” an SL Green spokesperson said in a statement to Commercial Observer. “There are no structural issues with the building, and we are already working with the licensed professional engineer of record to address this condition,” the spokesperson added. “We do not anticipate any impact to the overall project schedule, with other work ongoing, and have already submitted our request to rescind the partial stop work order.” While the Pfizer buckling certainly spurred a renewed scrutiny of ongoing conversion projects in New York City and an increased focus on safety, these types of partial stop-work orders are not uncommon. bullets: NYC DOB halted SL Green's $805M office-to-residential conversion at 750 Third Ave. (680 units, +11 floors).
Partial stop-work order issued after steel columns not properly welded; work above 8th floor suspended.
Third Manhattan conversion halt this month; prior incidents at 235 East 42nd (MetroLoft) and 222 Broadway.
stories.summary: New York City's Department of Buildings issued a partial stop-work order at SL Green Realty's $805 million office-to-residential conversion at 750 Third Avenue in Midtown East, which was designed to deliver 680 units across 11 new floors. Inspectors found improperly welded steel columns and inconsistencies, halting all steel work above the eighth floor. This marks the third Manhattan conversion halt in July, following structural failures at MetroLoft's 235 East 42nd Street and cracks at 222 Broadway.
stories.impact: Repeated structural failures on major Manhattan office conversions signal systemic execution and quality-control issues in the conversion pipeline, likely triggering extended DOB inspections citywide. This will materially delay delivery timelines and increase hard costs (rework, engineering review, inspection delays) for all active and planned conversion projects in Manhattan, reducing near-term residential supply relief and extending the window for traditional new construction to capture rent growth.

stories.title: New York Life Sees Leasing Momentum at 757 Third Ave. Amid Continued Renovations
stories.excerpt: JLL has completed 24,107 square feet of leasing activity at 757 Third Ave. The leasing activity comes as New York Life continues to enhance the Midtown East office property with planned cosmetic renovations to the lobby and the rollout of a new prebuilt office program. Rectn leases include the following: ● Financial services firm Dutchess Management expanded into the entire 24th floor, totaling 6,987 square feet. The tenant was represented by Mark Weiss and Jenna Catalon of Cushman & Wakefield. ● Yuco Management, a real estate development and management organization, signed a new full-floor lease for 6,960 square feet. The tenant, relocating from 200 Park Ave., was also represented by Weiss and Catalon. ● Elite signed a new full-floor lease totaling 6,960 square feet. Adam Ardise, Stephen Bellwood and Rachel Rosenfeld of Cushman & Wakefield represented the tenant. ● Real estate investment firm Wharton Equity Partners renewed its lease for 3,200 square feet. Wharton was represented by Jonathan Serko, Barry Zeller and Barry Garfinkle of Cushman & Wakefield. JLL serves as the agency leasing broker for 757 Third Ave. The team is led by vice chairman Mitch Konsker, executive managing director Clark Finney, senior managing director Simon Landmann, SVP Kristen Morgan and VP Lance Yasinsky. The post New York Life Sees Leasing Momentum at 757 Third Ave. Amid Continued Renovations appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: New York Life completed 24,107 SF of leasing at 757 Third Ave. (Midtown East office).
Four tenants signed leases; financial services and real estate firms dominate; one relocated from 200 Park Ave.
Landlord pursuing cosmetic renovations and new prebuilt office program to drive occupancy.
stories.summary: JLL brokered 24,107 square feet of leasing activity at 757 Third Ave. in Midtown East, including full-floor leases for Dutchess Management (6,987 SF), Yuco Management relocating from 200 Park Ave. (6,960 SF), and Elite (6,960 SF), plus a renewal by Wharton Equity Partners (3,200 SF). New York Life is enhancing the property with cosmetic renovations and a prebuilt office program to attract additional tenants.
stories.impact: Moderate leasing activity and tenant relocations from other Midtown locations suggest modest recovery in Manhattan office demand, but not yet a surge. While this confirms some flight-to-quality, broader multifamily implications are limited—continued office softness in secondary locations may modestly reduce job growth/migration tailwinds in Midtown East residential markets. Watch for whether prebuilt models accelerate subletting and block new demand.

stories.title: BGO, Yukon Real Estate Partners Sell 291K-SF Kansas Cold Storage Facility
stories.excerpt: BGO and Yukon Real Estate Partners announced the sale of New Century Cold Storage, a newly built 291,000-square-foot, plant-attached, rail-served cold storage warehouse in New Century, Kansas, to a MetLife Investment Management client. The facility, owned and co-developed through a joint venture between BGO and Yukon, was purpose-built as a plant-attached, build-to-suit warehouse for CJ Logistics America. “With its purpose-built design, strategic location, and direct integration with food production and logistics operations, we believe this facility will make a meaningful contribution to the strength and resilience of U.S. food supply chains for decades to come,” said Kevin Rivest, Managing Partner, BGO. The New Century facility is located within the Johnson County Airport Commission’s New Century AirCenter industrial park, with a direct rail spur to the building and access to the BNSF Railway transcontinental intermodal facility. The property is positioned less than four miles from Interstate 35. The post BGO, Yukon Real Estate Partners Sell 291K-SF Kansas Cold Storage Facility appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: BGO and Yukon sold New Century Cold Storage, 291K SF rail-served facility in Kansas to MetLife Investment Management client.
Plant-attached, build-to-suit warehouse purpose-built for CJ Logistics America in New Century AirCenter.
Industrial asset sale reflects investor demand for supply-chain-critical, purpose-built logistics infrastructure.
stories.summary: BGO and Yukon Real Estate Partners sold New Century Cold Storage, a newly constructed 291,000-square-foot rail-served cold storage warehouse in New Century, Kansas, to a MetLife Investment Management client. The facility was purpose-built as a plant-attached build-to-suit for CJ Logistics America within the Johnson County Airport Commission's New Century AirCenter industrial park. The transaction highlights investor appetite for strategically located, supply-chain-integrated logistics assets.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact on multifamily development. However, cold storage and logistics expansion in Kansas/Johnson County markets signals job growth in industrial/supply-chain sectors, which may drive population and wage growth in regional housing markets over time. Monitor for broader logistics hub consolidation in the Midwest and resulting residential demand.

stories.title: AI Platform Clay Leases 44K SF with Swig Company
stories.excerpt: The Swig Company has leased 44,000 square feet at The Mills Building to artificial intelligence platform Clay. The lease was announced two weeks after Swig refinanced the circa-1891 property at 220 Montgomery St. in San Francisco’s Financial District. “The Mills Building continues to attract companies seeking a workplace that reflects their culture and ambitions,” said Stacia Keisner, SVP of asset management at The Swig Company. “Clay’s lease is another example of an innovative business choosing downtown San Francisco to recruit talent, foster collaboration, and position themselves for long-term success.” Cory Kristoff, EVP, director of leasing, added, “Through our focused spec suite initiative at the Mills Building, we have leased more than 102,000 square feet of space year to date, representing approximately 21% of the property. We are encouraged by this strong leasing momentum and expect it to continue throughout the remainder of the year and beyond.” Bart O’Connor, Mark Geisreiter and Hannah Potter of Newmark represented The Swig Company. Maurice (Mo) Spikes, Derek Feinman and Aaron Ellison of Newmark represented Clay. The post AI Platform Clay Leases 44K SF with Swig Company appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: AI platform Clay leased 44K SF at Mills Building, 220 Montgomery St., San Francisco Financial District.
Swig Company has leased 102K+ SF YTD (21% of property); expects leasing momentum to continue.
Lease follows Swig's recent property refinancing; tech/AI tenant attraction supports downtown SF recovery narrative.
stories.summary: AI platform Clay signed a 44,000-square-foot lease at The Mills Building (circa-1891) in San Francisco's Financial District, brokered by Newmark. The Swig Company has leased over 102,000 square feet year-to-date (approximately 21% of the property) and expects continued momentum. The lease was announced two weeks after Swig refinanced the property, signaling improved credit availability and rising asset values in downtown San Francisco.
stories.impact: AI company expansion and spec-suite leasing momentum in downtown SF Financial District suggests renewed corporate demand and tech sector confidence in the submarket. This may drive talent in-migration and wage growth, strengthening residential demand in adjacent neighborhoods (SOMA, Mission Bay, South Beach). Watch for whether this catalyzes a broader downtown living trend and justifies new multifamily development in walkable SF submarkets.

stories.title: City Selects Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies to Build 980 Homes in LIC
stories.excerpt: A development team made up of Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies and Volunteers of America has been chosen to create nearly 1,000 new homes upon a vacant parcel in Long Island City, Queens. The 70,000-square-foot development, at 54-42 Second Street, will be called the Orion, and two-thirds of its units will be set aside as affordable housing. “It is exactly what New York needs,” David Schwartz, principal and co-founder of Slate Property Group, said in a statement. “And we look forward to working with City Hall to get shovels in the ground as soon as possible.” The parcel sits within the 30-acre Hunter’s Point South housing complex. When completed, Hunter’s Point South is expected to feature approximately 5,000 new homes, roughly 3,000 of which will be affordable. The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) began courting developers for the site, known as Parcel E, in June of last year. The request for proposals came with the requirement that Parcel E host more affordable homes than previous phases. The Orion will include approximately 980 new apartments. Two-thirds of the apartments, roughly 658 units, will be income-restricted, affordable to extremely low- to moderate-income households. Approximately 150 units will be set aside as supportive apartments. “Reaching households at every income level in a high-opportunity neighborhood like Hunter’s Point reflects a simple belief: Where New Yorkers live shouldn’t come down to income alone,” said Laszlo Syrop, principal and head of acquisitions at Hudson Companies. The mixed-use community, designed by Marvel Architects, will feature an affordable child care center, a workforce development center and a community pool. Approximately 6,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial retail space will also be made available along Second Street and Center Boulevard. bullets: Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies, Volunteers of America selected to build Orion: 980 homes in LIC (54-42 Second St.), Queens.
Two-thirds of units (≈653) set aside as affordable; project within 30-acre Hunter's Point South complex.
When complete, Hunter's Point South will feature ≈5,000 homes (≈3,000 affordable); city-driven development pipeline.
stories.summary: The city selected a developer team of Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies, and Volunteers of America to build the Orion, a 980-unit mixed-income residential project on a 70,000-square-foot parcel (54-42 Second St.) in Long Island City, Queens. Two-thirds of units will be affordable housing. The project is part of the larger 30-acre Hunter's Point South complex, which upon completion will feature approximately 5,000 homes, roughly 3,000 of which will be affordable.
stories.impact: Hunter's Point South represents a major city-driven multifamily delivery pipeline adding ~5,000 units to Queens over the next 5–7 years, with heavy affordable mandates that will suppress average rents in the submarket. Market-rate developers in LIC should target adjacent neighborhoods (Astoria, Ditmars, Dutch Kills) and focus on premium positioning to differentiate. Expect modest rent growth in LIC as supply inflates; stronger upside in undersupplied outer-Queens pockets.

stories.title: AI Infrastructure Firm Treeswift Signs 7K-SF Lease at 256 West 38th Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-driven infrastructure technology company is relocating its offices to Midtown. Philadelphia-based Treeswift signed a four-year, 7,487-square-foot lease on the entire 11th floor of the Hakimian Organization’s 256 West 38th Street in an expansion of its New York City operations, according to landlord broker Lee & Associates NYC. Asking rent was $39 per square foot. It is unclear where Treeswift is relocating from within New York City, but the company also has an office in Philadelphia. “Artificial intelligence companies have become one of the most active drivers of office leasing demand in Manhattan, but they are not all looking for trophy towers,” Lee & Associates’ Todd Korren, who represented the landlord alongside Noah Caspi, said in a statement. “As these businesses grow, they are seeking efficient, well-connected headquarters that support collaboration, attract talent and provide long-term value. Treeswift’s relocation reflects that trend.” Daniel Rodriguez Sains of Buchbinder Warren negotiated on behalf of the tenant and did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Treeswift specializes in helping clients with infrastructure inspections, vegetation management, construction planning, wildfire mitigation and storm response, according to the brokerage. The firm will move into its new offices at 256 West 38th Street in August. It’s unclear when the Rex Hakimian-led firm got involved in the building’s ownership, but his name starts showing up on deed filings sometime after March 2025, when Empire Capital Holdings acquired the property and nearby 229 West 36th Street in a state of distress for a steep discount at $50 million. The seller, Investcorp, purchased the two buildings for $157 million in 2017, Commercial Observer previously reported. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: AI infrastructure firm Treeswift signed 7,487 SF lease at 256 West 38th St., Midtown; $39/SF asking rent.
Four-year lease for entire 11th floor; Treeswift expanding NYC operations from Philadelphia base.
AI companies driving Manhattan office demand but seeking efficient, collaborative space outside trophy towers.
stories.summary: Philadelphia-based AI infrastructure technology company Treeswift signed a four-year, 7,487-square-foot lease on the entire 11th floor of 256 West 38th Street in Midtown at $39/SF asking rent, expanding its New York City operations. Lee & Associates noted that AI companies are increasingly active office drivers in Manhattan but are seeking efficient, well-connected headquarters outside trophy buildings to support collaboration and attract talent.
stories.impact: AI-driven office demand is absorbing secondary Midtown space at modest rents ($39/SF) and filtering talent into the submarket, supporting residential demand in nearby neighborhoods (Hell's Kitchen, Midtown West). However, this demand is insufficient to offset broader Manhattan office decline; multifamily developers should monitor whether AI clusters (West Midtown, Flatiron, Brooklyn Tech Triangle) create durable residential hubs worthy of new construction.

stories.title: PCCP, Stonemont Close on $1B-Plus Acquisition of Blackstone Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: PCCP and Stonemont Financial Group are officially the new owners of a 5.9 million-square-foot industrial portfolio, Commercial Observer can first report. The joint venture acquired the 38 assets, located across 14 markets in 10 states, for upward of $1 billion with Blackstone as the seller, according to an article from Real Estate Alert preceding the sale. The portfolio was sold via an off-market transaction, with Eastdil Secured serving as adviser, and the transaction closed July 29. It wasn’t immediately clear how the acquisition was financed. “The acquisition of this portfolio represents PCCP’s continued conviction in the industrial sector and in markets we have actively invested in within the last five years,” Ryan Dodge, a partner with PCCP, said. “We believe our industrial portfolio continues to exhibit strong momentum, with increased leasing demand in recent months. In our view, this portfolio is well positioned to benefit from those same market tailwinds.” The portfolio — leased to a diverse roster of more than 70 tenants — is located across infill submarkets, including Denver, Dallas, Atlanta, and Charlotte, N.C., as well as strong growth markets like San Diego, Reno, Nev., and El Paso, Texas. With PCCP and Stonemount Financial now in the driver’s seat, the JV’s plan is to focus on revenue growth via contractual rent increases and marking-to-market on leases that are being renewed, according to a release. “This transaction reflects our conviction in the long-term fundamentals of the industrial real estate sector,” said Zack Markwell, CEO and managing principal at Stonemont. “We are pleased to have once again partnered with PCCP and will continue to pursue attractive acquisition opportunities alongside our active development program.” The industrial sector is one of PCCP’s investment fortés, with the firm currently managing more than 68 million square feet of industrial assets over 52 markets. This acquisition brings its count to 262 industrial transactions.
bullets: PCCP and Stonemont acquired 5.9M SF industrial portfolio (38 assets, 14 markets, 10 states) from Blackstone for $1B+ on July 29.
Portfolio features diverse roster of tenants; off-market transaction brokered by Eastdil Secured.
Buyer cites strong leasing demand momentum and confidence in industrial sector and existing market footprints.
stories.summary: PCCP and Stonemont Financial Group closed the acquisition of a 5.9 million-square-foot industrial portfolio comprising 38 assets across 14 markets in 10 states for more than $1 billion, with Blackstone as the seller. The off-market transaction closed July 29, brokered by Eastdil Secured. PCCP cited strong recent leasing demand momentum and conviction in markets where the firm has actively invested over the past five years.
stories.impact: Mega-fund industrial acquisition signals continued investor confidence in logistics and supply-chain real estate, driven by durable e-commerce demand and post-COVID reshoring trends. This activity will likely push cap rates tighter and valuations higher, making speculative industrial development more attractive and competitive. Watch for secondary industrial submarkets (mid-tier metros in target markets) as acquisition targets, which may constrain land availability for alternative development, including multifamily.

stories.title: Fed Holds Interest Rates in Warsh’s Second Meeting as FOMC Chair
stories.excerpt: The second Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting under new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh signaled another reality check of higher-for-longer interest rates to the commercial real estate industry. In a 9-3 vote, the FOMC maintained its benchmark interest rate Wednesday at between 3.5 percent and 3.75 percent for the fifth straight meeting, citing inflation risks from ongoing war in Iran. Inflation remains well above the Fed’s 2 percent target at a time when Warsh has laid the groundwork for possibly changing its data approach when crafting monetary policy decisions. Warsh said in a post-meeting press conference that the FOMC doesn’t have a “soft target” for inflation and remains committed to the 2 percent annual rate as a chief goal. “We have begun a new chapter and we understand that the five-plus years of inflation above target cannot be cured in nine weeks or by a single month of modest price decreases,” Warsh said. “This Fed will not waver. Our credibility rests on performing our duties and delivering on our responsibilities.” The vote to maintain interest rates came with some dissent as FOMC regional presidents Beth M. Hammack of Cleveland, Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis and Lorie K. Logan of Dallas voted no, preferring instead to implement a quarter-point hike. Warsh’s second meeting leading the Fed after replacing Jerome Powell as chair in May occurred two weeks after he said during congressional testimony that the FOMC has “no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation.” Warsh also spoke to whether traditional inflation gauges such as the Consumer Price Index and the Producer Price Index (PPI) should be rethought. The new Fed chair appointed a task force in June that will examine whether the central bank’s long-standing inflation metrics needs to change, with findings expected later in the year. bullets: Federal Reserve (Chair Kevin Warsh) held benchmark rate at 3.5%–3.75% in 9-3 FOMC vote; fifth consecutive hold.
Warsh commits to 2% inflation target; cites ongoing Iran conflict as inflation risk; signals higher-for-longer stance.
Fed emphasizes that 5+ years of above-target inflation cannot be cured quickly; credibility hinges on persistence.
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve, in Chair Kevin Warsh's second FOMC meeting, voted 9-3 to maintain the benchmark interest rate at 3.5–3.75% for the fifth consecutive meeting, citing inflation risks from ongoing geopolitical conflict. Warsh reaffirmed the Fed's commitment to a 2% inflation target and signaled that persistently above-target inflation (now 5+ years) cannot be reversed quickly, emphasizing the Fed's credibility depends on not wavering.
stories.impact: Higher-for-longer interest-rate environment locks in elevated borrowing costs for construction financing and acquisition debt, materially compressing development feasibility and cap rates. Rising rates reduce leverage capacity and increase hurdle rates for underwriting, narrowing the set of viable projects to best-in-class locations with strong sponsorship. Expect continued moderate construction starts and selective underwriting; projects with floating-rate exposure face refinance pressure in 18–24 months.
